# Farm Management

You have given up programming and moved to the Sanjiang Plain to start farming. During your time working in the fields, you have adopted a regular daily schedule, and now you work **exactly** $$$m$$$ units of time each day. It is now harvest season, and you need to harvest and process $$$n$$$ types of crops. For crop type $$$i$$$, processing it for one unit of time will yield a profit of $$$w_i$$$. To make your daily work less monotonous, for each crop type $$$i$$$, the time spent processing it each day can range between $$$[l_i, r_i]$$$ inclusive as an integer.



At some day, the weather forecast says that there will be a heavy rain tomorrow and you can't work, so you need to adjust your schedule to quickly gather your crops today. Specifically, you can choose at most one type of crop and remove its daily time range restriction, allowing the time spent processing this crop to be any integer in the range $$$[0, m]$$$. The time ranges for all other crops remain unchanged. You have to work **exactly** $$$m$$$ units of time as well.



You want to determine the maximum profit you can earn today.



## Input



The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^5$$$, $$$1 \le m \le 10^{11}$$$), representing the number of crop types and the length of the workday in units of time, respectively.



The next $$$n$$$ lines each contain three integers $$$w_i$$$, $$$l_i$$$, and $$$r_i$$$ ($$$1 \le w_i \le 10^6$$$, $$$1 \le l_i \le r_i \le 10^6$$$), indicating the profits and time constraints of the crops.



It is guaranteed that $$$\sum_{i=1}^n l_i \le m \le \sum_{i=1}^n r_i$$$.



## Output



Output a single integer representing the maximum profit you can earn today.

# A Game On Tree

There is a tree (a connected undirected graph with $$$n$$$ nodes and $$$n-1$$$ edges) consisting of $$$n$$$ nodes, with nodes numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. Clearly, there is a unique simple path between any two nodes in the tree.



Xiaohong and Xiaolan are playing a game on this tree. In each game, both players **independently and uniformly** select a random simple path from all $$$\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$$$ simple paths (regardless of direction) that exist in the tree. Note that they may choose the same path. Let $$$X$$$ denote the number of edges that are common to both selected paths, and the score of the game is $$$X^2$$$.



Your task is to find the expected value of the score $$$E(X^2)$$$ when Xiaohong and Xiaolan play the game once, and output the result modulo $$$998244353$$$ (see the output format for details).



## Input



The first line contains a positive integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T \le 10^4$$$), representing the number of test cases.



For each test case, the first line contains a positive integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2\le n \le 10^5$$$), representing the number of nodes in the tree.



The next $$$n-1$$$ lines each contain two positive integers $$$u, v$$$ ($$$1\le u,v \le n$$$), indicating that there is an edge between nodes $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$. The input is guaranteed to be a tree.



The sum of all $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^6$$$.



## Output



For each test case, output a single integer, representing the answer modulo $$$998244353$$$.



Formally, let $$$M=998244353$$$. It can be shown that the answer can be expressed as an irreducible fraction $$$\frac p q$$$, where $$$p$$$ and $$$q$$$ are integers and $$$q \not\equiv 0\pmod M$$$. Output the integer equal to $$$p\cdot q^{-1}\pmod M$$$, where $$$q^{-1}$$$ denotes the modular multiplicative inverse of $$$q$$$ modulo $$$M$$$. In other words, output such an integer $$$x$$$ that $$$0\le x \lt M$$$ and $$$x\cdot q\equiv p\pmod M$$$. It can be proved that there is exactly one $$$x$$$ which meets the condition.



## Note



For the first test case in the example, the answer without taking the modulo is $$$\frac{10}{9}$$$.



Among the $$$9$$$ possible cases:



- In $$$2$$$ cases, the number of common edges between the two paths is $$$0$$$;

- In $$$6$$$ cases, the number of common edges between the two paths is $$$1$$$;

- In $$$1$$$ case, the number of common edges between the two paths is $$$2$$$.



Therefore, the answer is $$$E(X^2) = \frac{2 \cdot 0^2 + 6 \cdot 1^2 + 1 \cdot 2^2}{9} = \frac{10}{9}$$$.

# Counterfeit Money

Problem PA
Counterfeit Money
Time limit: 3 seconds
Memory limit: 1024 megabytes
Problem Description
The banknotes of the ICPC Kingdom have anti-counterfeiting measures. Each banknote has an
exclusive serial number, and this serial number is divisible by 13. In other words, if the serial
number is not divisible by 13, then the banknote is counterfeit. To verify whether a number is
divisible by 13, we can directly divide the number by 13. Yet, there is another method:
Partition the digits of the given decimal number into groups starting from the right, where
each group has three digits. Now, treat each group as a three-digit number. Then, from
the rightmost group, apply subtraction and addition operations alternately to the three-digit
number and obtain the result. If the result is divisible by 13, then the original number is
divisible by 13. Otherwise, it is not.
For example, for the number 123,456,789, if we apply subtraction and addition operations
alternately from the rightmost group of 3 digits, we get 789 − 456 + 123 = 456. As 456 is not
divisible by 13, the original number 123,456,789 is not divisible by 13.
For another example, for the number 593,825,856, if we apply subtraction and addition opera￾tions alternately from the rightmost group of 3 digits, we get 856 − 825 + 593 = 624. As 624
is divisible by 13 (624 = 13 × 48), the original number 593,825,856 is divisible by 13.
Based on the above method, write a program to verify whether a banknote is counterfeit or
not.
Input Format
The input contains several test cases. The first line stands for the number of test cases 𝑡. The
next 𝑡 lines will each contain a positive number. The given number may contain up to 1000
digits.
Output Format
For each input number, output the absolute value of the result when we apply the above
alternate-add-subtract method. Then, on the same line, output “YES” if the input number is
divisible by 13, and “NO” otherwise. There is a space between the output value and YES/NO.
1

Technical Specification
 1 ≤ 𝑡 ≤ 1000.
 Each input number may contain up to 1000 digits.
Sample Input 1
2
123456789
593825856
Sample Output 1
456 NO
624 YES
2

Problem PC
Where the Lantern Lights are Dimming
Time limit: 3 seconds
Memory limit: 1024 megabytes
Problem Description
The Lantern Festival features many lanterns on display. In the darkness of the night, they cast
beautiful shadows and reflections, attracting numerous visitors to come and go. With so many
lanterns on display simultaneously, it’s impossible to showcase the unique features of each. As
such, the organizers switch on the lights of some lanterns while turning off others in rotation.
At any given time, some lanterns are illuminated while others rest. Additionally, some lanterns
remain perpetually off due to malfunctions, missing their chance to dazzle.
To engage the visitors in the Lantern Festival, the organizers also hold a scoring event. If a
visitor is very satisfied with the festival, they will receive a pack of stickers worth 3 points
each, and they will affix one 3-point sticker to each lantern on display. If they feel satisfied,
they will receive a pack of 1-point stickers and place one on each displaying lantern. If they are
disappointed with the festival, they will get a pack of -2 point stickers and apply one to each
displaying lantern. In other words, those lanterns that are resting and not illuminated won’t
have an opportunity to receive any stickers from this visitor. After the festival ends, please
help write a program to calculate the total points from all the stickers on the lanterns.
Input Format
The input begins with a line containing two integers, 𝑛 and 𝑚. The next 𝑛 lines describe the
initial state of 𝑛 lanterns, numbered from 0 to 𝑛 − 1. Each of these lines contains two integers:
𝑠𝑖 and 𝑝𝑖
. 𝑠𝑖 represents the state of the lantern:
 1 if the 𝑖-th lantern is initially on,
 0 if it is off,
 -1 if it is out of order (meaning it is perpetually off and cannot be turned on)
𝑝𝑖
indicates the total points from stickers that are already on the 𝑖-th lantern.
The following 𝑚 lines represent 𝑚 events given in chronological order, each corresponding to
one of two even types: switching or scoring.
 Lines beginning with the letter W signify a switching event. They have two subsequent
integers, 𝑙𝑗 and 𝑟𝑗
, which imply that the state of lanterns numbered in the range [𝑙𝑗
, 𝑟𝑗
]
(inclusive) will be toggled.
1

 Lines beginning with the letter C denote a scoring event by a visitor. These lines have
a single subsequent integer, 𝑞𝑗 ∈ {−2, 1, 3}, indicating the sticker score assigned by the
visitor. Every lantern currently on display receives a sticker with 𝑞𝑗 points from the
visitor.
Output Format
Output a single integer that is the total points from all the lanterns after the festival.
Technical Specification
 1 ≤ 𝑛 ≤ 1, 000, 000
 1 ≤ 𝑚 ≤ 1, 000, 000
 𝑠𝑖 ∈ {−1, 0, 1}
 −10, 000 ≤ 𝑝𝑖 ≤ 10, 000
 0 ≤ 𝑙𝑗 ≤ 𝑟𝑗 < 𝑛
 𝑞𝑗 ∈ {−2, 1, 3}

3 3
0 0
0 0
0 0
W 0 2
W 1 1
C 3
Sample Output 1
6
Sample Input 2
5 5
1 5
0 0
-1 2
1 0
0 -2
C 1
W 0 4
C -2

C 3

9
2

# Quarantine Policy

Problem PD
Quarantine Policy
Time limit: 3 seconds
Memory limit: 1024 megabytes
Problem Description
The 2019 novel coronavirus, COVID-19, can be transmitted between humans through water
droplets and close contact. The transmission is especially easy and fast in relatively crowded
or confined spaces, such as airplanes or trains. If someone is infected with COVID-19, then
passengers occupying the adjacent seats will be infected easily.
To prevent the spread of the virus, we can take precautions, such as washing hands regularly
and avoiding touching our eyes, nose, or mouth, to avoid infection. In addition, governments
have also implemented special measures such as isolation and quarantine for this purpose. For
instance, when someone on an airplane caught the coronavirus, the person will need to be
isolated. Moreover, persons occupying the seats adjacent to the infected person will need to
be quarantined. Precisely, there are two types of adjacent seats. One is directly adjacent, that
is the seat is in the front, rear, left, or right of the virus seat. The other one is diagonally
adjacent, that is the seat is in the front-left, front-right, rear-left, or rear-right of the virus seat.
In the quarantine policy, someone whose seat is directly adjacent will be quarantined for 𝑑1
days, and someone whose seat is diagonally adjacent will be quarantined for 𝑑2 days. If there
is more than one infected person adjacent to some seat, the number of days of quarantine will
not be accumulated.
Please write a program to output which seats whose occupying persons need to be quarantined,
and the number of days of quarantine. If a seat whose occupying person needs to be quarantined
for different days, output the maximum of such days.
Input Format
The input contains several test cases. The first line stands for the number of test cases 𝑡. For
each test case, the first line contains four integers 𝑛, 𝑚, 𝑑1, 𝑑2 (0 < 𝑛, 𝑚 ≤ 100, 1 ≤ 𝑑2 ≤ 𝑑1 <

# Slabstones Rearrangement

Problem PE
Slabstones Rearrangement
Time limit: 3 seconds
Memory limit: 1024 megabytes
Problem Description
Babara has a garden. She has bought some rectangular slabstones and worked out an initial
placement of all slabstones in the garden. The shape of the garden is rectangular. An edge
of a slabstone should be either parallel or orthogonal to an edge of the garden. There exists a
slabstone touching the left, right, bottom, and top edges of the garden, respectively. All the
slabstones are contained in the garden. Meanwhile, none of the slabstones overlap in the initial
placement. Babara enjoys stepping slabstones from one to another every day. However, Babara
would like to redesign her garden to make room for some other purposes. She is wondering how
tight the slabstones can be packed together if they can only be shifted horizontally (i.e., left
or right) without changing their vertical coordinates. Furthermore, if the vertical dimensions
of any two slabstones overlap (not including touching of their ends), their relative locations in
the horizontal direction should be maintained. That is, if the vertical dimensions of slabstones
R and Q overlap and, before shifting, slabstone Q is on the right of slabstone R, Q should be
still on the right of R after shifting or vice versa. Besides, there is a minimal horizontal spacing
between two slabstones during slabstone rearrangement if their vertical dimensions overlap.
The slabstones should remain non-overlapping after shifting. Nevertheless, their horizontal
edges may touch. Now you are asked to help Babara calculate the largest area that can be
spared for other purposes.
Input Format
The first line holds an integer specifying the number of test cases. It is then followed by the
input data of the test cases. The first line of the input for each test case gives two integers.
The first one specifies the number of rectangular slabstones whereas the second one gives the
minimal horizontal spacing between two slabstones. Then, each of the following lines contains
four integers. The first two integers specify the initial x and y coordinates of the bottom-left
corner of a slabstone in the garden. The remaining two integers specify the initial x and y
coordinates of the top-right corner of a slabstone. Two adjacent numbers are separated by a
whitespace.
Output Format
The output of a test case takes a line. It contains the largest area saved by shifting the
slabstones. If no area can be saved, just output zero.
1

Technical Specification
 The number of test cases is not more than 32.
 All the coordinates are 32-bit unsigned integers.
 A garden’s area is not larger than the maximal 32-bit unsigned integer.
 The width and length of a slabstone are 32-bit unsigned integers. They should be larger
than zero.
 The minimal horizontal spacing between any two slabstones is a 32-bit unsigned integer
and should be greater than zero.
 The number of slabstones is from 4 to 100.
Sample Input 1
2
4 2
2 6 4 12
8 4 16 8
7 10 11 16
18 4 20 18
6 4
2 5 4 11
2 14 6 17
7 10 10 16
9 4 16 7
11 11 16 14
18 4 20 18
Sample Output 1
28
0
2

# Baker’s Dilemma

Problem PF
Baker’s Dilemma
Time limit: 3 seconds
Memory limit: 1024 megabytes
Problem Description
A baker has 𝑁 bakery orders from customers that he must fulfill, but he can only handle one
order a day. For the 𝑖
𝑡ℎ order, the baker needs to spend 𝐷𝑖 (1 ≤ 𝐷𝑖 ≤ 1000) consecutive days
to complete it; however, for every day of delay, the baker must be fined 𝑆𝑖 (1 ≤ 𝑆𝑖 ≤ 10000).
For example, if the baker receives four orders to make biscuits, the number of days required
for each order is 3, 1, 2, 5, and the penalty for each day of delay is 4, 1000, 2, 5. If the baker’s
work order is 1 2 3 4, the penalty will be 4×0 + 1000×3 + 2×4 + 5×6 = 3038, but if the work
order is 2 1 3 4, the penalty will be 1000×0+ 4×1+ 2×4+ 5×6. 0+ 4×1+ 2×4+ 5×6 = 42,
so the latter penalty is less. Please write a program to help the baker to find out the sequence
of work which has the least penalty.
Input Format
The first line of the input has a positive integer 𝑇 representing the number of groups of data.
Then, there are 𝑇 groups of data. For each group, the first line has an integer 𝑁 between 1 and
1000 representing the number of orders, followed by 𝑁 lines, each with two integers separated
by a space character, representing the number of days required for each order, 𝐷, and the
penalty, 𝑆, for each day of delay, in that order.
Output Format
For each set of data, output the sequence of jobs with the smallest penalty on one line. Each
job is represented by its number, separated by a blank character. If there is more than one set
of answers, print the one with the smallest dictionary order. Note that each group of jobs is
numbered starting with 1.
Technical Specification
 1 ≤ 𝑇 ≤ 1000.
 1 ≤ 𝑁 ≤ 1000.
 1 ≤ 𝐷𝑖 ≤ 1000, ∀1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑁.
 1 ≤ 𝑆𝑖 ≤ 10000, ∀1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑁.
1

Sample Input 1
2
4
3 4
1 1000
2 2
5 5
5
3 4
1 1000
8 8
2 2
5 6
Sample Output 1
2 1 3 4
2 1 5 3 4
2

Problem PK
Chemical Storage
Time limit: 1 second
Memory limit: 1024 megabytes
Problem Description
International Chemical Producing Company (ICPC) is an international company that
manufactures various chemicals. The company built several chemical rooms for storing chemi￾cals. They made a short railroad to connect two chemical rooms for convenience to move the
chemicals. The network of the chemical rooms and the railroads form a special tree graph in
which all the nodes are within distance 2 of a central path. We label each node a number
sequentially from 1. Fig. 1 gives an example of networks.
Figure 1: An example of networks with chemical rooms and railroads.
Each chemical product will be stored in a tank placed in a chemical room. Since the chemicals
may leak into the air, the safety rule is that the chemicals cannot be placed in two adjacent
rooms to avoid adverse chemical reactions between the chemicals. Fig. 2 gives two chemical
placement network examples: (a) is safety, and (b) is unsafety.
Figure 2: Two examples of chemical placement networks: (a) safety and (b) unsafety.
1

Sometimes, the workers must clean the tanks and move some chemicals to the other chemical
rooms. Peter is the worker, and his manager will assign him a task with two safety placement
networks: the source network 𝑇𝑠 and the destination network 𝑇𝑑. A task is called 𝑓𝑒𝑎𝑠𝑖𝑏𝑙𝑒
if a possible strategy exists to move the chemicals from 𝑇𝑠 to 𝑇𝑑 following the safety rules;
otherwise, it is called 𝑖𝑛𝑓𝑒𝑎𝑠𝑖𝑏𝑙𝑒. Notice that we do not restrict chemicals to be placed in a
specific room. If 𝑇𝑠 and 𝑇𝑑 are the same, the task is also treated as feasible. Fig. 3 and Fig. 4
show examples of feasible and infeasible tasks, respectively.
Figure 3: A feasible task: (a) the source network, (b) move the chemical from 4 to 5, (c) move
the chemical from 1 to 2, (d) move the chemical from 2 to 3, (e) move the chemical from 5 to
4 to the destination network.

Please write a program to help Peter judge whether a task is feasible or not.
2

# Bouncing Particles

Bouncing Particles
Input file: standard input
Output file: standard output
Time limit: 2 seconds
Memory limit: 1024 megabytes
This problem has an attachment. You can use it to simulate and visualize the movements
of the particles.
VegiCat observes particles on a grid with n rows and n columns. The lower-left cell has coordinates (1, 1).
The horizontal coordinate increases from left to right, and the vertical coordinate increases from bottom
to top. Each particle has a horizontal direction (left or right) and a vertical direction (up or down). At
the beginning of each step, each particle adjusts its directions as follows:
• Its horizontal direction is reversed if the next cell in that direction is outside the grid.
• Its vertical direction is reversed if the next cell in that direction is outside the grid.
After these adjustments, a particle at (x, y) produces two child particles:
• One at (x − 1, y) if its horizontal direction is left, or at (x + 1, y) if it is right;
• One at (x, y − 1) if its vertical direction is down, or at (x, y + 1) if it is up.
Both child particles inherit the parent’s horizontal and vertical directions. The parent then disappears.
Multiple particles may occupy the same cell at the same time, regardless of their directions. They do not
interact or change each other’s directions.
At time 0, there are four particles at (x0, y0), with the following direction pairs:
• Right and up;
• Left and up;
• Right and down;
• Left and down.
At each step, all particles simultaneously adjust their directions and then split as described above.
You are given q queries. Each query gives integers A, B, C and a time t. For each query, find the number
of grid cells (x, y) that satisfy Ax + By + C = 0 and contain at least one particle at time t.
Input
The first line contains an integer T (1 ≤ T ≤ 105
), the number of test cases. The description of the test
cases follows.
The first line of each test case contains four integers n, x0, y0, q (2 ≤ n ≤ 109
, 1 ≤ x0, y0 ≤ n, 1 ≤ q ≤ 105
).
The grid has n rows and n columns. The initial cell is (x0, y0), and there are q queries.
Each of the next q lines contains four integers A, B, C and t (|A|, |B|, |C| ≤ 109
, 0 ≤ t ≤ 109
). This
describes a query for the line Ax + By + C = 0 at time t. It is guaranteed that A and B are not both 0
simultaneously.
It is guaranteed that the sum of q over all test cases does not exceed 105
.
Output
For each query, output one integer on one line: the number of grid cells (x, y) that satisfy Ax+By+C = 0
and contain at least one particle at time t.
Page 1 of 2

standard input standard output
1
6 5 5 4
2 -1 -5 0
1 -1 0 1
11 45 14 2
1 0 -5 3
1
0
0
3

# Counting Arrays

VegiCat gives you two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$. Consider integer arrays $$$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$$$ such that



$$$$$$a_1=0,\qquad 0\le a_{i+1}-a_i\le 1\quad(1\le i \lt n).$$$$$$



Let $$$s_i=a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_i$$$ be the prefix sums of $$$a$$$. VegiCat also tells you the prefix sums at $$$m$$$ positions; that is, you are given $$$m$$$ constraints of the form $$$s_{p_j}=v_j$$$ ($$$1\le j\le m$$$).



Count the number of arrays satisfying all constraints, modulo $$$998244353$$$. If no array satisfies all the constraints, the answer is $$$0$$$.



## Input



The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le 10^4$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



Each test case is given as follows:



The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1\le n\le100$$$, $$$0\le m\le n$$$), the length of the array and the number of prefix sum constraints, respectively.



The $$$j$$$-th of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains two integers $$$p_j$$$ and $$$v_j$$$ ($$$1\le p_j\le n$$$, $$$0\le v_j\le10^9$$$). This describes a constraint: the sum of the first $$$p_j$$$ elements of the array must equal $$$v_j$$$.



The positions $$$p_j$$$ are given in strictly increasing order.



## Output



For each test case, output an integer — the number of valid arrays modulo $$$998244353$$$.



## Note



Without any prefix constraints there are exactly $$$2^{n-1}$$$ such arrays, because each of the $$$n-1$$$ adjacent differences may independently be $$$0$$$ or $$$1$$$.



In the second test case, the only array with $$$s_3=1$$$ is $$$(0,0,1)$$$.



In the third test case, $$$s_2=0$$$ forces $$$a_2=0$$$, after which $$$a_3$$$ may be $$$0$$$ or $$$1$$$.



In the fourth test case, the arrays are $$$(0,1,1,1)$$$ and $$$(0,0,1,2)$$$.



In the fifth test case, the arrays with $$$s_5=4$$$ are $$$(0,0,1,1,2)$$$ and $$$(0,1,1,1,1)$$$.



In the sixth test case, $$$s_2=0$$$ forces $$$a_1=a_2=0$$$, so $$$s_5\le6$$$. The constraint $$$s_5=10$$$ is impossible.
content.title: Counting Arrays

# Duel of Wrath

VegiCat and VegiDog are playing a special duel in Slay the Spire. VegiCat plays as Watcher A, and VegiDog plays as Watcher B. A and B have base attack powers $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ and initial health values $$$h_A$$$ and $$$h_B$$$, respectively.



At the start of each round, the game determines each Watcher's stance for that round. Each Watcher can be in one of the following two stances:



- Normal: damage dealt and damage received are unchanged.

- Wrath: damage dealt and damage received are both doubled.



For each attack, the damage initially equals the attacker's base attack power. It is doubled if the attacker is in Wrath and doubled again if the defender is in Wrath. Thus, the damage in each round is as follows:



- If both characters are in Normal, A deals $$$a$$$ damage to B, and B deals $$$b$$$ damage to A.

- If exactly one character is in Wrath, A deals $$$2a$$$ damage to B, and B deals $$$2b$$$ damage to A.

- If both characters are in Wrath, A deals $$$4a$$$ damage to B, and B deals $$$4b$$$ damage to A.



Each round, both characters attack once simultaneously, and both health values decrease simultaneously. Both attacks take effect even if either character's health becomes $$$0$$$ or less during the round. At the end of the round, a character with health less than or equal to $$$0$$$ dies. If either character dies, the battle ends immediately; otherwise, the next round begins. Base attack powers never change, and health is never restored.



The stances for each round are determined by the game, not by the players. Any combination of the two characters' stances is possible in each round.



VegiCat wins only if B dies while A remains alive. If both characters die in the same round, VegiCat does not win. Determine whether VegiCat will win **regardless of how both characters' stances change**.



## Input



The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1 \le T \le 10^5$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



Each test case contains one line with four integers $$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, $$$h_A$$$, and $$$h_B$$$ ($$$1 \le a,b,h_A,h_B \le 10^{18}$$$), giving the characters' base attack powers and initial health values, respectively.



## Output



For each test case, output `YES` if VegiCat will win regardless of how both characters' stances change, and `NO` otherwise. Output each answer on a separate line.



You can output the answer in any case. For example, `yEs`, `yes`, `Yes`, and `YES` are all accepted as positive responses.



## Note



In the first test case of the first sample, B always dies in the first round. A receives at most $$$4$$$ damage in that round and remains alive.



In the second test case of the first sample, A wins if both characters are normal in the first round. If both characters are in Wrath in the first round, both die. Therefore, the answer is `NO`.

# Enclose the Point

There are $$$n$$$ points $$$P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$$$ in the plane. VegiCat has $$$q$$$ queries for you. Each query gives a point $$$P$$$.



For each query, construct a simple polygon using some of the given points as its vertices. The polygon must contain $$$P$$$ **strictly** inside it and have the **minimum number of vertices**. If no such polygon exists, output $$$-1$$$.



A simple polygon is a closed polygonal chain with at least three distinct vertices. Adjacent edges intersect only at their common endpoint, and nonadjacent edges do not intersect.

 ![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/2364c910aad508a7ff1ae1de18cb4f60dad739ca.png) Examples of simple and non-simple polygons



## Input



The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le 2\cdot 10^4$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



The first line of each test case contains two positive integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$3\le n\le 10^5$$$, $$$1\le q\le 10^5$$$), representing the number of given points and the number of queries.



The $$$i$$$-th of the next $$$n$$$ lines contains two integers $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ ($$$-10^9\le x_i,y_i\le 10^9$$$), the coordinates of $$$P_i$$$. It is guaranteed that these $$$n$$$ points are pairwise distinct.



Each of the next $$$q$$$ lines contains two integers $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$ ($$$-10^9\le x,y\le 10^9$$$), the coordinates of the queried point.



It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^5$$$.



It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$q$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^5$$$.



## Output



For each query, if no polygon satisfying the requirements exists, output one integer $$$-1$$$ on a line.



Otherwise, output a polygon with the minimum number of vertices. On the first line, output one integer $$$m$$$, the number of vertices.



On the second line, output $$$m$$$ integers $$$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_m$$$ ($$$1\le a_i\le n$$$), the indices of the vertices in order. The polygon is $$$P_{a_1}P_{a_2}\ldots P_{a_m}$$$. The vertices may be output in either clockwise or counterclockwise order.



The indices must be pairwise distinct, and the output polygon must be simple and contain the queried point strictly inside it. If there are multiple solutions, output any of them.



## Note



In the first test case, the triangle $$$P_4P_1P_2$$$ contains the queried point $$$P=(0,0)$$$ strictly inside it. Since a polygon has at least three vertices, this triangle has the minimum number of vertices.



In the second test case, the only possible polygon is the triangle $$$P_1P_2P_3$$$. The queried point $$$P=(0,0)$$$ lies on the edge $$$P_2P_3$$$, so the answer is $$$-1$$$.

# Graph Reconstruction

VegiCat has an $$$n\times n$$$ integer matrix $$$A=(a_{ij})$$$. For each $$$1\le i,j\le n$$$:



- If $$$i=j$$$, $$$i=1$$$, or $$$j=1$$$, then $$$a_{ij}=-1$$$.

- Otherwise, $$$a_{ij}$$$ is a nonnegative integer.



Help VegiCat construct an undirected simple graph $$$G$$$ with $$$n$$$ vertices, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$.



For every pair of distinct vertices $$$i,j$$$ with $$$i \gt 1$$$ and $$$j \gt 1$$$, the graph must satisfy the following condition: after deleting vertices $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$, together with all edges that have an endpoint at either vertex, exactly $$$a_{ij}$$$ edges must remain.



Each pair of vertices $$$i,j$$$ is considered separately. That is, for each pair, start with $$$G$$$ before any vertices or edges have been deleted.



It is guaranteed that at least one such graph exists. If there are multiple solutions, output any of them.



## Input



The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le 6\cdot 10^4$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



For each test case, the first line contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$4\le n\le 10^3$$$), denoting the number of vertices in the graph.



Then each of the next $$$n$$$ lines contains $$$n$$$ space-separated integers $$$a_{ij}$$$ ($$$-1\le a_{ij}\le \frac{(n-3)(n-2)}{2}$$$), representing the matrix $$$A$$$ described in the statement.



It is guaranteed that the total sum of $$$n^2$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$1.2\cdot 10^6$$$, and that at least one graph corresponding to matrix $$$A$$$ exists.



## Output



For each test case, output the adjacency matrix of the graph you construct. Output $$$n$$$ lines, each containing $$$n$$$ space-separated integers. Each integer must be either $$$0$$$ or $$$1$$$. The entry in the $$$i$$$-th row and $$$j$$$-th column is $$$1$$$ if there is an edge between vertices $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$, and $$$0$$$ otherwise. If there are multiple solutions, output any of them.



## Note



The actual input matrix will only have a single space between two integers. The extra spaces in the sample are designed to enhance the readability of the layout.

# Hidden Order

**This is an interactive problem.**



VegiCat knows an array $$$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$$$, where each element is $$$0$$$, $$$1$$$, or $$$2$$$. He does not want to tell you its values, but you can ask him questions. In each query, you choose two indices $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$, and VegiCat tells you whether $$$a_i \gt a_j$$$.



VegiCat asks you to output the indices in nondecreasing order of the corresponding array values. That is, find a permutation $$$p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n$$$ of $$$1,2,\ldots,n$$$ such that $$$$$$ a_{p_1}\le a_{p_2}\le\cdots\le a_{p_n}. $$$$$$



You may make at most $$$2n-3$$$ queries in each test case.



**The interactor is adaptive.** This means that the array is not fixed in advance. The interactor guarantees that there always exists at least one array with elements in $$$\{0,1,2\}$$$ consistent with all responses given so far. Your final permutation must be valid for **every array consistent with all responses**.



## Input



The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le 250$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



Each test case begins with an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2\le n\le 500$$$), the length of the array.



The sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$500$$$.



## Interaction



To make a query, output a line in the following format:



```text

? i j
```



Here, $$$1\le i,j\le n$$$. After each query, read one integer:



- $$$1$$$, if $$$a_i \gt a_j$$$;

- $$$0$$$, if $$$a_i\le a_j$$$.



Queries with $$$i=j$$$ and repeated queries are allowed and are included in the query count.



When you have determined the order, output a line in the following format:



```text

! p_1 p_2 ... p_n
```



Each index from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ must appear exactly once. Printing the answer does not count as a query.



If your answer is correct, proceed to the next test case by reading its $$$n$$$, or terminate your program if this was the last test case. The interactor does not send a separate confirmation after an answer.



After outputting each query or answer, output a newline and flush the output buffer. To flush your output, you can use:



- `fflush(stdout)` or `cout.flush()` in C/C++;

- `System.out.flush()` in Java and Kotlin;

- `sys.stdout.flush()` in Python.



If you make an invalid query, exceed the query limit, or print an incorrect answer, you will receive a **Wrong Answer** verdict. Output that does not follow the specified format is also judged **Wrong Answer**. In these cases, the interactor terminates without sending an error response.



## Note



In the first test case, the queries ? 1 2 and ? 2 3 both return $$$1$$$, so $$$a_1 \gt a_2 \gt a_3$$$. Therefore, $$$(3,2,1)$$$ is a correct answer.



In the second test case, the query ? 1 2 returns $$$0$$$, so $$$a_1\le a_2$$$. Therefore, $$$(1,2)$$$ is a correct answer.

# Invisible Edges

**This is a multi-pass problem.**



VegiCat and VegiDog play a game with a forest of $$$n$$$ vertices, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, and $$$m$$$ edges. A forest is an undirected graph with no cycles. It is **not necessarily connected**.



In the first stage, VegiCat assigns an integer $$$a_u$$$ ($$$1\le a_u\le 2n$$$) to each vertex $$$u$$$. The values may repeat.



After VegiCat finishes assigning the values, the vertices are renumbered. Let $$$p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n$$$ be a permutation of $$$1,2,\ldots,n$$$, in which each integer from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ appears exactly once. For each $$$u$$$, the vertex originally numbered $$$u$$$ is now numbered $$$p_u$$$.



Each edge $$$(u,v)$$$ becomes $$$(p_u,p_v)$$$. Each vertex keeps its assigned value. Let $$$b_i$$$ be the value at vertex $$$i$$$ after renumbering. Then $$$b_{p_u}=a_u$$$.



In the second stage, VegiDog receives only $$$n$$$ and $$$b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n$$$, without the original forest or $$$p$$$. He must recover all edges using the new vertex numbers.



Design strategies for both players that work for every valid forest and every permutation $$$p$$$.



## Input



Your program will run twice: first as VegiCat, then as VegiDog. The test cases appear in the same order in both runs.



**First Run.** The first line contains the string `cat`, indicating that you play VegiCat.



The second line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le 10^4$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1\le n\le 2\cdot 10^5$$$, $$$0\le m \lt n$$$), the number of vertices and edges.



Each of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1\le u,v\le n$$$, $$$u\ne v$$$), describing an undirected edge between vertices $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$.



It is guaranteed that the graph has no cycles or multiple edges.



It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2\cdot 10^5$$$.



**Second Run.** The first line contains the string `dog`, indicating that you play VegiDog.



The second line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le 10^4$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



The first line of each test case contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1\le n\le 2\cdot 10^5$$$), the number of vertices.



The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n$$$ ($$$1\le b_i\le 2n$$$), the assigned values in the new vertex order.



It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2\cdot 10^5$$$.



## Output



**First Run.** For each test case, output $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$$$ ($$$1\le a_i\le 2n$$$) on one line. The integer $$$a_i$$$ is the value assigned to vertex $$$i$$$.



**Second Run.** For each test case, output an integer $$$m$$$ on the first line, the number of edges. Each of the next $$$m$$$ lines must contain two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1\le u,v\le n$$$, $$$u\ne v$$$), describing an edge using the new vertex numbers.



Output each edge once, in any order. Either endpoint may come first. If $$$m=0$$$, output only $$$0$$$.



## Note



In the first test case, the forest has one vertex and no edges. VegiCat assigns the value $$$1$$$ to the vertex, and VegiDog outputs $$$0$$$.



In the last test case, the permutation is $$$p=[5,3,6,4,2,9,1,8,7,10]$$$.



VegiCat assigns $$$a_7=16$$$. Since $$$p_7=1$$$, VegiDog receives $$$b_1=16$$$.



The original edge $$$(3,7)$$$ becomes $$$(p_3,p_7)=(6,1)$$$.



The original edge $$$(4,10)$$$ becomes $$$(p_4,p_{10})=(4,10)$$$. The sample outputs this edge as $$$(10,4)$$$, which represents the same undirected edge.



The sample illustrates the input and output formats. Its outputs are correct for the graphs and permutations shown. However, the sample assignments are not guaranteed to be part of a strategy that works for every valid forest and every permutation.

# Joint Relocation

VegiCat owns a company with $$$n$$$ employees in $$$k$$$ nonempty teams. The employees live along a straight road, represented by a number line. VegiCat wants to arrange two meeting points for them.



VegiCat divides the teams into two sets, $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$, with each team in exactly one set. He chooses a meeting point for each set at any real coordinate. **All employees on the same team must go to the same meeting point.** Each team in set $$$A$$$ goes to the meeting point for $$$A$$$, and each team in set $$$B$$$ goes to the meeting point for $$$B$$$. Either set may be empty.



Let $$$S_A$$$ list the home positions of all employees on teams in $$$A$$$, and define $$$S_B$$$ similarly for $$$B$$$. Each employee is counted separately, even when home positions repeat.



For a list $$$S=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_m)$$$ of home positions, the minimum total distance for these employees to travel to one meeting point is $$$$$$ M(S)=\min_{p\in\mathbb{R}}\sum_{j=1}^{m}|x_j-p|. $$$$$$ Define $$$M(S)=0$$$ when $$$S$$$ is empty. Help VegiCat minimize $$$M(S_A)+M(S_B)$$$ over all ways to divide the teams into the two sets.



## Input



The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le 3\cdot10^5$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1\le k\le n\le 3\cdot10^5$$$), denoting the number of employees and the number of teams, respectively.



Each of the next $$$k$$$ lines describes one team. The $$$i$$$-th line contains an integer $$$m_i$$$ ($$$1\le m_i\le n$$$), the number of employees on team $$$i$$$, followed by $$$m_i$$$ integers $$$x_{i,1},\ldots,x_{i,m_i}$$$ ($$$1\le x_{i,j}\le10^7$$$), their home positions. The sum of all $$$m_i$$$ in a test case is $$$n$$$.



Home positions may repeat and may be given in any order.



It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$3\cdot10^5$$$.



## Output



For each test case, output an integer — the minimum possible total travel distance.



## Note



In the first test case, VegiCat sends team $$$1$$$ to a meeting point at position $$$1$$$ and team $$$2$$$ to a meeting point at position $$$8$$$. The employees in each team travel a total distance of $$$2$$$, giving the answer $$$4$$$.



In the second test case, VegiCat chooses meeting points at $$$3$$$ and $$$9$$$. He sends teams $$$1$$$ and $$$2$$$ to the first meeting point, and team $$$3$$$ to the second. The employees in teams $$$1$$$, $$$2$$$, and $$$3$$$ travel total distances of $$$12$$$, $$$1$$$, and $$$2$$$, respectively, giving the answer $$$15$$$.

# Keep Your Distance

VegiCat is on a mine-sweeping mission. There are $$$n$$$ mines on a number line. Mine $$$i$$$ is at the integer coordinate $$$a_i$$$. The mines are numbered in order of their coordinates, so $$$a_1\le a_2\le\cdots\le a_n$$$. Mine coordinates may repeat.



VegiCat tests each mine once, in the order $$$1,2,\ldots,n$$$. For mine $$$i$$$, he chooses an integer coordinate $$$b_i$$$ as the test location, which may be negative or zero. The error of this test is $$$|a_i-b_i|$$$.



For each $$$2\le i\le n$$$, an integer $$$l_i$$$ is given, specifying the minimum required distance between the test locations for mines $$$i-1$$$ and $$$i$$$. These locations must satisfy $$$$$$ |b_i-b_{i-1}| \ge l_i. $$$$$$



Help VegiCat minimize the largest test error; that is, find $$$$$$ \min_{\substack{ b_1,\ldots,b_n\in\mathbb{Z}\\ |b_i-b_{i-1}|\ge l_i\quad(2\le i\le n) }} \left(\max_{1\le i\le n}|a_i-b_i|\right). $$$$$$



## Input



The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1 \le T \le 10^4$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



The first line of each test case contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 10^5$$$), the number of mines.



The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$$$ ($$$1\le a_i\le10^9$$$), where $$$a_i$$$ is the coordinate of mine $$$i$$$. It is guaranteed that $$$a_1\le a_2\le\cdots\le a_n$$$.



The third line contains $$$n-1$$$ integers $$$l_2,l_3,\dots,l_n$$$ ($$$1 \le l_i \le 10^9$$$), where $$$l_i$$$ is the minimum distance between the test locations for mines $$$i-1$$$ and $$$i$$$.



It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^5$$$.



## Output



For each test case, output an integer — the minimum possible value of the largest test error.



## Note



In the first test case, choosing $$$b_1=1$$$ and $$$b_2=2$$$ gives a maximum error of $$$1$$$. An error of $$$0$$$ would require $$$b_1=b_2=1$$$, which violates the distance requirement.



In the second test case, one optimal choice is $$$b=[-4,7,15,10,8,22,13]$$$. All required distances are satisfied, and the maximum error is $$$6$$$.

# Long Slides

**This problem has an attachment. You can use it to simulate and visualize the movements of the robot.**



VegiCat has a robot on an infinite two-dimensional grid. He wants it to move from cell $$$s=(s_x,s_y)$$$ to cell $$$t=(t_x,t_y)$$$. Each cell has integer coordinates. The cells $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$ may be the same.



The robot follows a string $$$p$$$ of instructions. Each character is `L`, `R`, `U`, or `D`. Let $$$|p|$$$ denote the length of $$$p$$$.



The robot starts at $$$s$$$. Before it executes any instructions, you may place at most $$$|p|$$$ obstacles in distinct cells. The coordinates $$$(x,y)$$$ of each obstacle must satisfy $$$-2\cdot10^9 \le x,y \le 2\cdot10^9$$$. Neither $$$s$$$ nor $$$t$$$ may contain an obstacle. Each obstacle occupies one cell and remains fixed throughout the process; all other cells are free of obstacles.



The robot executes the instructions $$$p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_{|p|}$$$ in order. For each instruction, starting from its current cell $$$(x,y)$$$, it moves along the following sequence of cells:



- `L`: $$$(x,y)\to(x-1,y)\to(x-2,y)\to\cdots$$$;

- `R`: $$$(x,y)\to(x+1,y)\to(x+2,y)\to\cdots$$$;

- `U`: $$$(x,y)\to(x,y+1)\to(x,y+2)\to\cdots$$$;

- `D`: $$$(x,y)\to(x,y-1)\to(x,y-2)\to\cdots$$$.

 The robot repeatedly takes one step in the specified direction while the next cell contains no obstacle. It stops in the cell immediately before the first obstacle in that direction. If the next cell in the specified direction already contains an obstacle before the instruction starts, the robot stays in place, but the instruction is still completed. If there is no obstacle ahead in that direction, the robot would move forever, and the placement is invalid.

The robot may reach $$$t$$$ before all instructions are completed. It **must still execute all remaining instructions**. Construct any obstacle placement satisfying the requirements above such that the robot finishes at $$$t$$$ after the last instruction, or report that no such placement exists.



## Input



The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1 \le T \le 10^5$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$s_x$$$ and $$$s_y$$$ ($$$-10^9\le s_x,s_y\le10^9$$$), the coordinates of the starting cell.

The third line contains the instruction string $$$p$$$ ($$$1 \le |p| \le 10^5$$$), consisting only of the characters `L`, `R`, `U`, and `D`.



It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$|p|$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^5$$$.



## Output



For each test case, output an answer in input order. Obstacle placements for different test cases are independent.



If no valid placement exists, output `NO` on a line by itself.



Otherwise, output `YES` on the first line. On the second line, output an integer $$$k$$$ ($$$0\le k\le|p|$$$), the number of obstacles.

All $$$k$$$ coordinate pairs must be distinct, and none may equal $$$s$$$ or $$$t$$$. The placement must allow every instruction to finish and leave the robot at $$$t$$$ after the last instruction. If there are multiple solutions, output any of them.



You can output the yes or no verdict in any case. For example, `yEs`, `yes`, `Yes`, and `YES` are all accepted as positive responses.

# Minimum Records

VegiCat has $$$n$$$ closed integer intervals $$$[l_1,r_1],[l_2,r_2],\ldots,[l_n,r_n]$$$.



He wants to construct a sequence $$$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$$$ by choosing an integer $$$a_i$$$ from each interval $$$[l_i,r_i]$$$. That is, $$$l_i\le a_i\le r_i$$$ for every $$$1\le i\le n$$$.



A position $$$i$$$ is called a **record position** if $$$a_i \gt a_j$$$ for every $$$1\le j \lt i$$$. In particular, position $$$1$$$ is always a record position.



Help VegiCat minimize the number of record positions. Output this minimum number.



## Input



The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le 10^4$$$), the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows.



The first line of each test case contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1\le n\le 10^6$$$), the number of intervals.



The $$$i$$$-th of the next $$$n$$$ lines contains two integers $$$l_i,r_i$$$ ($$$-10^9\le l_i\le r_i\le 10^9$$$), describing the interval available at position $$$i$$$.



It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^6$$$.



## Output



For each test case, output an integer — the minimum possible number of record positions.



## Note



In the first test case, one optimal sequence is $$$a=[1,100,20,30]$$$. Its record positions are $$$1$$$ and $$$2$$$.



In the second test case, one optimal sequence is $$$a=[-1,4,1,2,8,6,12,12]$$$. Its record positions are $$$1$$$, $$$2$$$, $$$5$$$, and $$$7$$$. Position $$$8$$$ is not a record because its value equals the maximum seen so far.

Problem F. Turtle Soup
Time limit: 1 second

A company consists of n members with employee IDs 1, 2,...,n. Member 1 is the boss, and every other
member i (2 → i → n) has a direct supervisor fi (1 → fi <i). The company structure forms a rooted tree
with member 1 at the root.
In this company, member a knows member b if and only if at least one of the following conditions is
satisfied:
• a = b.
• b is an ancestor of a. In other words, there exists a sequence u1,u2, ··· ,uk (2 → k) such that
u1 = a, uk = b, and ui = fui→1 for all 2 → i → k.
• b is a direct child of a (b is a direct subordinate of a). In other words, fb = a.
Note that the acquaintance relationship is not necessarily symmetric; a knowing b does not imply that b
knows a.
Now, members are playing a game. In each round, a specific member m acts as the guesser, and another
member p is the target. It is guaranteed that p is a member whom m does not know.
To identify p, m asks a sequence of questions. For each question, m chooses an ID x and asks: “Does p
know member x?” Member p always answers truthfully. Additionally, if x = p, p will specifically reveal
that they are member x, at which point the game ends.
Each question carries a travel cost based on the company tree. If the i-th question concerns member
xi, the cost of that question is dis(xi→1,xi), where dis(a, b) is the number of edges on the unique path
between a and b in the tree. For the first question (i =1), the cost is dis(m, x1).
Member m is extremely clever and uses an optimal strategy to minimize the total cost required to
guarantee the completion of the game in the worst-case scenario. Your task is to calculate this minimum
worst-case cost for every possible guesser m ↑ {1, 2,...,n}.
If a member m already knows everyone in the company, the answer for that m is 0.

The first line of the input contains an integer n (1 → n → 105), representing the total number of members
in the company.
The second line contains n ↓ 1 integers, representing f2,f3, ··· ,fn. It satisfies 1 → fi <i.
Output
Output a single line containing n integers, representing the answers for the cases where
m =1,m =2, ··· ,m = n. The integers should be separated by spaces.

022

43344

435446

To explain the case of m =4 in sample 3: First, as shown in the diagram, member m does not know
membes {3, 5, 6}. One possible optimal strategy is to first ask if member 2 is known by p, costing 1. If so,
it indicates that p =5, and the next step is to ask about member 5 to end the game, with a total cost

by a letter according to its shape: I, T, O, J, L, S, and Z. Players receive a tetromino each time and need
to place it in a certain position.
However, the tetrominoes that players receive are not completely random. Instead, every 7 distinct
tetrominoes are grouped into a bag, and at the start of the game, players will receive each tetromino
in the first bag in sequence, followed by each tetromino in the second bag, and so on. The order of
receiving tetrominoes within each bag is completely random, and the order between bags is completely
independent. This method of receiving tetrominoes is referred to as the 7-BAG.
In this problem, we are not limited to the 7 di!erent tetrominoes, but rather consider a more general
case where there are n di!erent tetrominoes, and the method of receiving tetrominoes is n-BAG (i.e.,

bag being completely independent). Each tetromino is numbered from 1 to n, and we have the following

Problem M. Reduction and Growth
Time limit: 2 seconds
Memory limit: 1024 megabytes
Consider two positive integer variables a and b. We define a “reduction” operation: D(a, b) means changing
the value of variable a to a
gcd(a,b) , while the value of b remains unchanged. Here, gcd(a, b) denotes the
greatest common divisor of a and b. For example, if a =6 and b = 10, then after calling D(a, b) once, the
value of a becomes 3, while b remains 10.
Consider a tree with positive integer vertex weights, where the vertex weight of node i is ci. We define
a“chain reduction” operation on the tree: Tu,v(a). Here, u and v are two nodes in the tree, and a is
a positive integer variable. Let’s assume that the simple path from u to v in the tree visits the nodes
x1,x2,...,xk (where 1 → k, x1 = u, and xk = v). The operation Tu,v(a) means performing the D(a, cxi )
operation in order from i =1 to k, that is, using the vertex weights along the path to reduce the value of
variable a sequentially.
Consider a tree R that initially has only one vertex, labeled 1, with a vertex weight of c1. To grow it into
a tree with n nodes, you need to perform n ↑ 1 growth operations. In the i-th operation, three integers
ai,ui,vi are given, where ui and vi are guaranteed to be nodes currently in the tree, and ai is an integer
variable. You need to first perform a chain reduction operation Tui,vi (ai), and then add a new node to
the tree: this new node is labeled i +1, its weight ci+1 is the value of ai after the chain reduction, and it
is connected to node vi.
Finally, please output the vertex weights of each node as the answer.

Output one line containing n positive integers, separated by spaces, representing the weights c1,c2,...,cn

小 ε 和小 ω 是两个珍惜彼此相伴时光的女孩子。小 ω 正在为小 ε 准备一份礼物，

小 ω 告诉了小 ε 每个问题的答案，其中第 i 个问题的答案为 zi，即小 ω 告诉小 ε
数列 a 满足 axi AND ayi = zi，其中 x AND y 表示 x 和 y 的按位与的值。
小 ε 感觉自己被小 ω 调戏了，怀疑小 ω 只是在胡乱回答她，可能满足以上条件的
数列 a 并不存在！
因此她找到了你，你需要告诉小 ε 满足上述条件的数列 a 是否存在。进一步地，小
ε 还想知道，如果这样的数列 a 存在，它的所有元素之和的最小可能值是多少。

k

个问题及其答案，注意 xi
, yi 可能相等。

对于每组测试数据，若合法的 a 不存在则输出 ‐1，否则输出一行一个非负整数，表

5 2 3 1
6 3 2 30
